cards.q: Name the six SI base quantities used in A-level Physics, with their units.
cards.a: Mass (kg), length (m), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K) and amount of substance (mol).
cards.why: Every other unit, such as the newton or the joule, is derived from these.

cards.q: Express the newton in SI base units.
Express the joule in SI base units.
cards.why: From work = force × distance: \(\text{kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m}\).

cards.q: State the powers of ten for the prefixes k, M, G and T.
State the powers of ten for the prefixes c, m, μ, n, p and f.
Convert 1 kW h into joules.
cards.a: \(3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}\)
steps: 1 kW h is the energy transferred at 1 kW for 1 hour.

cards.q: What is a random error, and how is its effect reduced?
cards.a: An error that makes readings scatter unpredictably above and below the true value. Its effect is reduced by repeating the measurement and taking a mean.

cards.q: What is a systematic error?
cards.a: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction. Repeating and averaging does not reduce it.
cards.why: It is removed by correcting the cause, such as recalibrating the instrument, or by using a graph's gradient.

cards.q: What is a zero error?
cards.a: A systematic error in which an instrument gives a non-zero reading when the true value is zero.
cards.why: Check for it before measuring, and subtract it from every reading.

cards.q: What does it mean to say a measurement is accurate?
cards.a: It is close to the true value.

cards.q: What does it mean to say a set of measurements is precise?
cards.a: The repeated readings are close to one another: there is very little spread about the mean.
cards.why: Precise readings need not be accurate: a systematic error can shift them all.

cards.q: What is the resolution of a measuring instrument?
cards.a: The smallest change in the quantity that the instrument can detect: the smallest non-zero reading it can show.

cards.q: What is the difference between repeatable and reproducible results?
cards.a: Repeatable: the same person, with the same method and equipment, gets the same results again. Reproducible: a different person, or a different method or equipment, gets the same results.

cards.q: A student writes: "Using a micrometer instead of a ruler makes the result more accurate." Which word should have been used?
cards.a: A micrometer has a better resolution, which reduces the uncertainty in the reading. Whether the result is accurate depends on how close it is to the true value, which a zero error could still spoil.

cards.q: A length is measured with a ruler marked in millimetres. Why is its uncertainty usually taken as ±1 mm, and not ±0.5 mm?
cards.a: Measuring a length takes two readings, one at each end, each with an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. The two uncertainties add.

cards.q: How is the uncertainty in a mean estimated from a set of repeated readings?
cards.a: As half the range of the readings.
cards.why: Leave out any anomalous reading before finding the mean and the range.

cards.q: A potential difference is measured as \(4.2 \pm 0.1\ \text{V}\). Calculate its percentage uncertainty.
cards.a: 2.4%

cards.q: Two quantities are added or subtracted. How are their uncertainties combined?
cards.a: Add the absolute uncertainties.
cards.why: This applies even when subtracting: uncertainties never cancel.

cards.q: A spring's length changes from \(10.0 \pm 0.5\ \text{cm}\) to \(25.0 \pm 0.5\ \text{cm}\). State its extension, with its absolute uncertainty.
cards.a: \(15.0 \pm 1.0\ \text{cm}\)
steps: The quantities are subtracted, so add the absolute uncertainties: \(0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0\ \text{cm}\).
cards.why: The difference of two readings has a larger percentage uncertainty than either reading.

cards.q: Two quantities are multiplied or divided. How are their uncertainties combined?
cards.a: Add the percentage uncertainties.

cards.q: A quantity is raised to a power, such as \(r^{2}\) or \(\sqrt{T}\). What happens to its percentage uncertainty?
cards.a: Multiply the percentage uncertainty by the power: by 2 for a square, by \(\frac{1}{2}\) for a square root.

cards.q: The density of a cube is found from its mass (percentage uncertainty 2%) and the length of one side (percentage uncertainty 1%). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the density.
cards.a: 5%
steps: Volume is the side cubed, so its percentage uncertainty is \(3 \times 1\% = 3\%\).
Density is mass ÷ volume, so add the percentage uncertainties.

cards.q: Why is it better to time 20 oscillations of a pendulum than to time one?
cards.a: The absolute uncertainty in the timing is the same, but it is spread over 20 oscillations, so the percentage uncertainty in the period is much smaller.

cards.q: What does an error bar on a graph point show?
cards.a: The uncertainty in that data point: the true value is expected to lie within the bar.

answerFigure.alt: Five plotted points on a graph, each with a vertical error bar, and a straight line of best fit that passes through every bar.

cards.q: How is the uncertainty in the gradient of a straight-line graph found?
cards.a: Draw the line of best fit and the worst acceptable line (the steepest or shallowest line that still passes through the error bars). The uncertainty is the difference between their two gradients.

answerFigure.alt: Five plotted points with error bars and two straight lines: the line of best fit, and a steeper dashed worst acceptable line that still passes through every error bar.

cards.q: Data in a calculation are given to 2, 3 and 4 significant figures. To how many significant figures should the final answer be given?
cards.a: 2 significant figures: the same as the least precise piece of data.
cards.why: Keep extra figures during the working and round only at the end.

cards.q: What is meant by an estimate to the nearest order of magnitude?
cards.a: A value given to the nearest power of ten.

cards.q: State the order of magnitude of the diameter of an atom, and of a nucleus.
cards.a: Atom: about \(10^{-10}\ \text{m}\). Nucleus: about \(10^{-15}\ \text{m}\).
cards.why: The atom is about a hundred thousand times wider than its nucleus.

cards.q: Estimate the weight of an apple, to the nearest order of magnitude.
cards.a: About 1 N
steps: Estimate the mass: an apple is about 0.1 kg.
cards.why: For an estimate, round \(g\) to \(10\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\) and state the value you assumed.
